newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe's financial elite try to quash EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: Europe's financial elite try to quash EMU doubts.

text.p: Leading European financial policy makers sought on Monday to stamp out growing speculation that European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) was floundering and would have to be delayed.

At a banking ceremony in Frankfurt, the president of the powerful Bundesbank, the present and future heads of the European Monetary Institute and others sang a common tune -- monetary union will go ahead as planned on January 1, 1999.
"All rumours referring to EMU delay are not in line with reality," the head of the German central bank, Hans Tietmeyer told reporters. "I consider a discussion about the timetable wrong."
Tietmeyer's views were supported later in the day by his fellow council member Ernst Welteke, who said that any delay in EMU would have the negative effect of giving a sharp boost to the German mark.

"The collapse of the starting date could have negative consequences, particularly for Germany, as we would then have to expect a sharp rise in the mark," Welteke said in a speech at a conference in the northern German town of Kiel.

Worries that EMU would have to be postponed have been mounting for weeks as it has become increasingly apparent that many countries, including Germany, are having difficulty qualifying for monetary union, especially when it comes to triming budget deficits.

Only last Friday, European financial markets were swept by rumour that a two-year delay in EMU was soon to be announced, forcing the Bundesbank and German finance ministry to offer calming statements.
Welteke said that while he was unsure whether Germany would be able to fulfill the budget deficit goal, there was "no necessity" as yet to start thinking about a delay in monetary union.
European Monetary Institute president Alexandre Lamfalussy also added a voice of reassurance, stressing EMU was on track.
"All these market rumours about a delay are unfounded," Lamfalussy told reporters at the conference.

One of the keys to whether EMU will happen on schedule is if Germany can slash its budget deficit to three percent of gross national product by next spring when the participants for EMU are selected. It was 3.9 pct in 1996.
German Finance minister Theo Waigel maintains that the country will meet the target but many private economists see the budget deficit clearly over the three percent threshold.

Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg, the president-designate of the EMI and a leading candidate to head the future European Central Bank stressed, however, that Germany would in the end qualify for EMU.
"I am confident that Germany will make it," he said.
Tietmeyer added he thought Germany had a good chance of qualifying, saying he was confident that the German economy would pick up "at the lastest by the spring."
Stronger German growth would increase tax revenues and reduce record long unemployment lines, helping Bonn get its fiscal house in order.
Germany is considered an essential member of monetary union, but other nations having difficulty qualifying for EMU drew more guarded support from policy-makers here.

Asked by an Italian television reporter if it were true whether Germany did not want Italy in EMU, Tietmeyer replied, "That is completely untrue. I would be delighted for Italy to join currency union, but it must meet the criteria."

Tietmeyer earlier told reporters it was important for countries trying to get into EMU to achieve a genuine reduction of their deficits and not simply a result which showed a good figure on paper but was the result of accounting tricks. "Accounting tricks do not resolve problems," he said.
Duisenberg, meanwhile, warned that a number of nations will not be able to qualify for EMU, despite efforts to slash deficits and reduce inflation.
"Nevertheless we must make allowance for the fact that a number of them will not be able to participate when EMU takes off on January 1, 1999, Duisenberg said.

The lone voice raising doubts about the EMU start-date was Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, who said that Germany, seen by many as the cornerstone of the whole EMU project, was unlikely to meet the criteria without further fiscal measures and he was not certain EMU would start on time.

Kuehbacher, in an interview with the Berliner Zeitung to be published on Tuesday, said that Germany was unlikely to meet the three percent deficit target unless Bonn passes a law to raise taxes or slash social spending.
